summaries.Good news: Today's uplifting stories celebrate nature's recovery and human ingenuity working in harmony—from tiny bamboo bridges doubling crab populations in Taiwan to kiwi birds returning to Wellington after a century, and American Indian schools hitting record graduation rates.
summaries.Ideas: The day's big-picture stories grapple with AI's rising costs hitting Wall Street, the erosion of corporate AI hype as productivity gains stall, and emerging tools helping ordinary people understand and resist unwanted AI in their daily lives.
summaries.Technology: Breakthrough hardware keeps pushing boundaries—from plant-based wound dressings delivering antibiotics autonomously, to China's ambitious satellite networks and autonomous buses reshaping transportation globally, while regulatory tensions simmer around robotics and innovation.
summaries.Design: Architecture and product design are boldly embracing nature-inspired forms and sustainable innovation, from Shenzhen's landscape-mimicking museum to grown bacterial lamps, while hospitals and small everyday objects like pencil cases prove that thoughtful design transforms how we live and heal.

items.title: This fast-growing field is helping scientists pinpoint climate change’s impact on weather events
items.snippet:
When a devastating heat wave, hurricane, flood or wildfire strikes, people often want to know: How much did human-caused climate change influence this event, if at all?



For many years, scientists could answer that question only in general terms. They knew that human-caused climate change was incr
items.line: Attribution science now lets us pinpoint climate change's fingerprints on specific weather disasters, moving from abstract warnings to concrete accountability.

items.title: Don’t like AI being forced on you? These librarians have the perfect first step
items.snippet: It’s built into your phone. Into your email. Into your search engine. Artificial intelligence is everywhere—to the point that avoiding it seems nigh on impossible. But there are ways to disable or ignore AI features, and librarians around the world are teaching their tech-averse patrons the ropes.
items.line: Librarians around the world are teaching people how to disable and resist unwanted AI features—reclaiming agency in an increasingly automated world.

items.title: Why Scientists Redesigned the Botox Enzyme With AI
items.snippet:
Researchers say AI vastly improves a technique used to engineer proteins. As a proof of concept, they redesigned the Botox enzyme to snip a protein linked to ALS.
The post Why Scientists Redesigned the Botox Enzyme With AI appeared first on SingularityHub.
items.line: Using AI to redesign the Botox enzyme for ALS treatment shows how computational protein engineering can repurpose existing molecules for breakthrough therapeutics.
